questions.stem: A bank's mortgage pre-assessment assistant reads applicant documents and returns a recommendation. The sponsor's launch criterion is ‘at least 90% agreement with underwriter decisions’, and the model scores 93% on a 400-case eval set. Six weeks in production, 6% of recommendations have been rejected on review, and the rejections are concentrated in applicants with two incomes and self-employed income. What does the architect say about the metric?

options.text: The metric is an aggregate over a population that hides the failure, so it needs to be decomposed by applicant profile with per-group floors, not just an overall bar — because an overall 93% can be produced by excellent performance on common cases and failure on the segment that matters.
The metric is fine; the eval set of 400 cases is simply too small, so the team should rebuild the eval set with 4,000 cases and re-measure before drawing any conclusion.

The metric is wrong because agreement with underwriter decisions is the wrong target — the team should measure whether each extracted field is correct against the source document, since that is what the model is actually doing.
The metric is correct but stale, since it was computed against the model available at launch; the team should re-run the eval against the current model to get a comparable baseline.

questions.explanation: An aggregate metric reports the mean over the population, and the stem's evidence is exactly the case where that hides a real defect: 6% production rejection concentrated in a specific profile means the overall 93% is being carried by the easy majority. The architect's response is to **decompose the metric by group and set per-group floors**, because a bar that can be cleared by compensating errors elsewhere is not a safety property. This matters more here than in most domains: two-income and self-employed cases are where underwriting judgement is hardest and where an error has regulatory and fairness consequences. Note the pattern in the distractors — all three assume the number or the method is stale, when the number is measuring the right thing at the wrong granularity.

whyWrong.B: A larger eval set reduces sampling noise, which is worth having, but it does not change what an average measures. If the eval set is drawn from the same population as the 400 cases, a 4,000-case average still conceals a failing subgroup — it just conceals it more precisely.
whyWrong.C: Field-level accuracy against the source document is the right metric for the *extraction* step and would be a good sub-metric, but it is not a substitute for the end-to-end recommendation: a recommendation can have every field correct and still be wrong once the underwriter's reasoning about how the fields combine is applied. Replacing the end metric with a component metric is how a system passes its eval and fails in production.
whyWrong.D: Re-running against the current model is good hygiene and it is not the diagnosis. The evidence describes a *production* rejection pattern by applicant profile — that is a data-distribution finding, and re-measuring the same aggregate on the same eval set would return essentially the same number.

questions.mindset: An overall average can hide a failing subgroup — decompose quality metrics by segment and set per-group floors, not just a global bar.

questions.stem: A support platform promises customers ‘replies start appearing within 3 seconds’. The dashboard shows mean time to first token of 1.9 seconds and has done for six months, while about 4% of sessions feel slow to customers and two enterprise accounts have complained. Which metric design does the architect recommend?

options.text: Measure the **distribution** — p95 time to first token plus the share of sessions above the 3-second threshold — because a mean over a right-skewed distribution hides exactly the slow tail that produces complaints, and the threshold is the number the customer-facing promise actually turns on.
Keep the mean but add a median, since the median is a better central measure for skewed latency data and is enough to characterise the experience.
Measure total end-to-end response time rather than time to first token, because customers experience the whole answer rather than the first token.
Keep time to first token but exclude sessions involving tool calls, since tool latency is an integration concern rather than a model-experience concern.

questions.explanation: Latency distributions are right-skewed — most requests are fast and a minority are slow — so the mean sits comfortably inside the fast mass and moves very little when the tail degrades. Six months of a flat 1.9-second mean alongside rising complaints is the signature of that. (A) fixes it on both counts: a **percentile** characterises the tail, and a **threshold exceedance rate** is directly the promise being made, which is what makes it actionable — you can alert on it and hold a release against it. Anthropic's latency guidance is explicit that averages hide the slow tail and that percentile and threshold metrics are what should be tracked. The distractors are each a partial improvement that leaves the tail invisible.

whyWrong.B: Adding a median is a genuine improvement and it is what an experienced engineer proposes first — but the median describes the middle of the distribution, so a session that takes 30 seconds barely registers. With 4% of sessions slow, both the mean and the median can sit under 2 seconds while the customer experience is deteriorating. You need the tail, not a better centre.
whyWrong.C: Total end-to-end time is a real metric and it matters for throughput and cost, but it is not the promise — the promise is that replies *start appearing* within 3 seconds. Substituting total time measures a different question and would let a system that shows nothing for 20 seconds and then finishes instantly pass.
whyWrong.D: Excluding tool-call sessions is the wrong instinct and it removes exactly the population that is complaining. Tool latency dominates the tail in most agentic systems, so excluding it means the dashboard describes only the easy sessions — which is how a real problem stays invisible for six months.

questions.mindset: Latency is right-skewed, so track percentiles and threshold-exceedance rates — an average hides the slow tail that produces complaints.

questions.stem: A team is choosing success criteria for a Claude-based invoice processor before any prompt work begins. Which set is MOST defensible?

options.text: Field-level accuracy per field type against a labelled set, straight-through-processing rate on the documents that currently need no human touch, cost per document, and p95 processing latency — all measured against the current manual process as a baseline.
A single ‘accuracy’ number over the labelled set, because one clear metric is easier to report to the steering group than four.
The percentage of invoices processed without human intervention, because that is the number the business cares about.
Agreement between the model's output and the output of the previous rules-based system, because that system is already trusted and its output is free to obtain.

questions.explanation: Success criteria written before the work starts do three jobs: they define the **target**, they become the **eval metric**, and they become the **production monitor**. (A) satisfies all three and, crucially, sets them against the current process — so ‘better’ has a referent. Field-level accuracy per field type matters because the fields differ wildly in difficulty and an overall average hides a catastrophic failure on the one field that carries the money. Straight-through-processing rate is the operational metric the business will actually feel, and cost and latency are the constraints that decide whether the design is viable at volume. This is the pattern from Anthropic's guidance on defining success: decide the criteria before tuning, and choose metrics that reflect the task rather than a proxy.

whyWrong.B: One number is easier to report and less useful to build. ‘Accuracy— a single number over the whole labelled set — cannot tell you whether a future prompt change helped the hard fields or broke the easy ones, and it is not traceable to any operational outcome. Four metrics is not reporting overhead; it is the information a decision needs.
whyWrong.C: Straight-through-processing rate is a genuinely important metric and it is included in (A) — but on its own it hides *why* documents fail. A system that processes 60% without help because it routes ambiguous cases to a human has the same number as one that reads documents accurately and needs help only when genuinely unclear, and the two call for completely different next steps.
whyWrong.D: Agreement with the existing system is a cheap, automatable metric and it is measuring the wrong target. The rules engine is being replaced because it fails in known ways, so agreement with it rewards reproducing its failures; and its output is free to obtain but not a definition of correct. Where a legacy system is a reasonable baseline it is one of several criteria, never the only one.

questions.mindset: Write success criteria before tuning: a target, an eval metric and a production monitor, all measured against today's baseline.

questions.stem: An insurance group wants one dashboard number for its claims-drafting assistant, to be reported to the board monthly. The assistant drafts letters that adjusters either accept, edit or reject, and a rejection carries a reason code. Which design does the architect recommend?

options.text: Report a small set of numbers that each answer a different question — accept rate, edit distance on accepted drafts, rejection rate by reason code, and the share of drafts escalated to a human — with the edit and rejection figures broken out by claim type, because a single blended number cannot be acted on.
Report an accept rate as a single headline number, since adjusters' acceptance is the most direct available signal and a single figure is what a board can hold in mind.
Report the share of drafts that reach a human untouched, since that is the strictest measure of automation and the least gameable.
Report the average number of characters an adjuster changes in an accepted draft, since edit distance is a continuous, sensitive measure and averages are preferable to rates.

questions.explanation: The purpose of a reported metric is to make the **next decision obvious**, and that requires a set that separates the different reasons a draft might be wrong. (A) does that: accept rate is the headline, but edit distance tells you the drafts are being accepted with substantial changes — which is a very different situation from clean acceptance — and rejection-by-reason-code points at the specific defect to fix, whether that is a missing clause, a wrong figure or a tone problem. Breakouts by claim type stop the aggregate from hiding a failing segment. The rejection reason code is already in the system, which is exactly the point: instrumentation that already exists should be used rather than a proxy invented.

whyWrong.B: Accept rate is the right headline and it is the weakest possible sole metric. It is easily gamed by an assistant that declines to say anything controversial, and it conflates ‘correct as written’ with ‘the adjuster did not object’ — an adjuster under time pressure accepts and fixes a wrong date. Without edit distance and reason-coded rejections, a decline in quality can hide behind a stable accept rate.
whyWrong.C: Untouched drafts measure how willing adjusters are to leave work alone, not whether it is right. It penalises any draft that is *almost* right and therefore heavily edited into rightness — which is often the most valuable case — and in a workflow with quality review this number can be near zero while the system is genuinely useful. It also inverts the incentive: the safest strategy is to write nothing.
whyWrong.D: Edit distance is a good, sensitive measure and it belongs on the dashboard. As the sole metric it is misleading: a large average can mean many small fixes or one catastrophic rewrite, and it rewards producing a near-empty draft that the adjuster must write from scratch. Rates by reason code are what localise the defect; a mean edit distance only tells you something is wrong.

questions.mindset: A reported metric must make the next decision obvious — report accept rate, edit distance and reason-coded rejections separately, not one blended number.

questions.stem: A legal-tech company's contract-review feature produces a multi-paragraph risk summary, so there is no single right answer. The team has 300 real contracts with summaries written by two associates, and an LLM judge that scores completeness 1-5 against a rubric. The judge agreed with an expert panel on 79% of summaries. Which TWO changes would MOST improve confidence in the resulting score? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have the human panel re-score the cases where the judge disagreed, and use those to sharpen the rubric — then re-run the judge, since a 79% agreement figure only becomes a usable measurement once you know what the disagreement is made of.
Use the two associates' summaries as the reference answers and score with exact match, since two independent professionals are a better ground truth than a panel of three.
Replace the LLM judge with a model from a newer generation, since judge agreement of 79% is primarily a limitation of the grading model's capability.
Report the 79% agreement figure alongside the feature's score and state the caveat, so consumers can interpret the number rather than treating it as ground truth.

Score the feature with a deterministic rubric — a checklist of required findings, each verified as present or absent in the output — which removes grader variability for the part of the task that is actually checkable.

questions.explanation: LLM-as-judge is legitimate and useful, but its score is only as meaningful as its **calibration**, and 79% agreement with an expert panel is a warning that has to be acted on rather than reported around. (A) is the calibration loop: the disagreements are the highest-information cases in the whole set, and reviewing them tells you whether the judge is strict, lenient or reading a different definition of ‘complete’ — after which the rubric improves and the agreement figure becomes a real measurement. (E) goes further and is the better answer where it applies: much of ‘completeness’ on a risk summary is genuinely **checkable** — did it identify the change-of-control clause, the uncapped liability, the auto-renewal term — and a deterministic checklist for that part is reproducible, free at 300-document scale, and immune to grader drift. Anthropic's eval guidance is explicit that LLM grading works best against a detailed written rubric and that its agreement with human judgement should be measured, not assumed.

whyWrong.B: Two associates writing summaries is not gold standard — it is two more samples, and they will disagree with each other on exactly the judgement calls the judge is being measured on. Anchoring on them also quietly redefines the target as ‘what a mid-level associate writes’ rather than ‘what a complete risk summary contains’, and exact match against prose is unusable anyway.
whyWrong.C: A newer grading model is worth evaluating, and it is not what the 79% figure diagnoses. The number tells you the judge disagrees with experts 21% of the time; it does not tell you whether that is a capability ceiling, a different reading of the rubric, or variance. Upgrading the grader without looking at the disagreements repeats the same measurement at a different price point.
whyWrong.D: Reporting the caveat is honest and it is not an improvement in confidence — it is a disclosure attached to an uncalibrated number. A 1-5 score whose grader agrees with experts 79% of the time has a wide and unknown error band, and consumers reading a dashboard will not carry that uncertainty. The two correct options make the number trustworthy; this one makes it caveated.

questions.mindset: An LLM judge is a measurement instrument — calibrate it against humans on the disagreements, and move whatever part of the rubric is objectively checkable into code.

questions.stem: An architecture group is designing the first eval set for a Claude-based support agent that resolves IT tickets. They have three months before a go/no-go decision and no budget for expert annotation. Which dataset design is MOST defensible?

options.text: Build a first set from a stratified sample of real historical tickets labelled by the support team who handled them, deliberately over-representing the rare and expensive categories, then grow it continuously by adding every production case a human had to take over — so the set reflects real traffic and concentrates where errors cost most.
Generate 2,000 synthetic tickets with an LLM covering plausible intents, difficulties and edge cases, and use those as the eval set, since scale matters more than realism for a first benchmark.
Have the agent itself generate its own training and eval examples from documentation, then grade its answers, since this requires no annotation budget and scales indefinitely.

Build a large set of 5,000 tickets labelled by running a second Claude instance over each one and keeping the output where both instances agree, since agreement between two runs is a sound proxy for correctness.

questions.explanation: An eval set has one job — predict production behaviour — so it has to be **drawn from the real distribution and labelled against what actually happened**. (A) gets both halves right: the support team who resolved a ticket knows the right answer at no annotation cost, and stratifying to over-represent rare expensive categories is what stops a set of mostly password resets from reporting a flattering average. The second half matters just as much: a production case that a human had to take over is a **naturally occurring failure**, so folding those in continuously is how the set stays current without a labelling project. Anthropic's guidance is to start from real data and log what happens in production, rather than to synthesise.

whyWrong.B: Synthetic tickets scale cheaply and they are useful for **stress-testing edge cases** — but a set generated by a model reflects that model's idea of what tickets look like, so it systematically misses the real distribution: the internal jargon, the malformed requests, and the specific categories that dominate actual volume. It is a good complement to a real set, not a replacement, and it cannot tell you the production pass rate.
whyWrong.C: This is the most tempting option because it costs nothing and sounds rigorous, and it fails on both ends at once. Agent-generated examples encode the agent's current understanding, so the eval set inherits exactly the blind spots you are trying to find; and an agent grading its own answer is not an independent measurement. The result is a number that moves with the system rather than tracking it.
whyWrong.D: Agreement between two model runs measures **consistency**, not correctness. Where two runs differ, that is information the design throws away — the disagreement cases are the ones worth human eyes. Anthropic's eval guidance is explicit that self-consistency is a distinct property from accuracy, and using it as a label produces a set that is confidently wrong in exactly the places the model is uncertain.

questions.mindset: Build the eval set from real traffic, over-represent rare expensive cases, label it from what actually happened, and keep adding production takeovers.

questions.stem: A healthcare provider's agent must complete a nine-step patient-intake flow: verify identity, confirm insurance, record medications, schedule appointments, update records, and so on. Some steps are read-only, some write to the EHR, and one requires a clinician's confirmation. The team has 60 completed intake sessions with per-step outcomes. Which test design BEST evaluates whether the agent can complete the flow correctly?

options.text: Evaluate at the level of the flow, with per-step assertions: did the correct steps run in an order consistent with their dependencies, did each write land in the right record with the right values, and did the clinician-confirmation step stop and wait? Use repeated trials per task because agent runs vary.
Evaluate whether the final record is correct at the end of the session, since the outcome is what matters to the patient and intermediate differences in ordering are harmless.
Evaluate each step in isolation with a hand-written unit test per step, so that a failure points unambiguously at one step and can be fixed independently.
Evaluate with an LLM judge scoring whether the transcript shows the intake was completed satisfactorily, since the flow involves language-heavy steps that deterministic assertions cannot capture.

questions.explanation: A multi-step flow has two distinct correctness properties and (A) is the only design that measures both. **Did the right things happen?** Each write must land in the right record with the right values — checkable against the system state. **Did they happen in a safe order?** Steps have dependencies, and a flow that reaches the right end state by running the EHR write before the insurance check has a defect the end state does not show. And the clinician-confirmation step is a **governance assertion**: it must be observed stopping and waiting, which is a specific, checkable behaviour. The final point is the one that surprises people — repeated trials per task — because agent runs vary, so a single pass measures luck as much as capability. Anthropic's eval guidance treats agent tasks as trials with pass rates, not one-shot assertions.

whyWrong.B: End-state checking is necessary but not sufficient, and in healthcare the insufficiency is not academic: an intake that writes to the EHR before insurance verification, or that proceeds past a clinician-confirmation step and fills it in afterwards, can reach a correct-looking final record having violated a control. A metric that cannot distinguish those two runs will report the unsafe one as a pass.
whyWrong.C: Per-step unit tests are the right instinct for the deterministic steps and they are valuable — but an agent flow's failures are overwhelmingly **emergent**: the agent chooses which steps to run, in what order, and with what arguments. A test that calls each step directly with known inputs never exercises the choice logic, which is the part most likely to be wrong.
whyWrong.D: An LLM judge is a reasonable tool and this option is attractive because the flow is conversational. But the properties that matter here are not stylistic — they are whether a write happened, with what values, in what order, and whether a confirmation was actually awaited — and none of those are reliably assessable from a transcript by a grader that cannot see system state. Use deterministic assertions for those, and reserve the judge for genuinely qualitative aspects such as tone.

questions.mindset: Evaluate an agent flow at the level of the flow: per-step assertions on writes and ordering, explicit checks that a human-confirmation step waited, and repeated trials.

questions.stem: A team evaluates a Claude-based classifier on a labelled set of 1,200 cases and wants to release a prompt change that scores 1.5 points higher. What does Anthropic's guidance say about the significance of a difference like this?

options.text: Treat the difference as meaningful only with a stated confidence or significance check rather than by the point estimate alone — because on a finite eval set a 1.5-point gap is within the range that sampling variation alone can produce, and a release decision needs to know which it is.
Treat any improvement as real, since the same labelled set was used for both versions, so the comparison is controlled and the direction is trustworthy.
Treat the difference as noise and require a 10-point improvement, since differences below 10% on a labelled set are conventionally ignored in classification work.
Release the change if the higher score is statistically significant at 95% confidence, and do not release otherwise, since that is the standard decision rule.

questions.explanation: Using the same labelled set removes one source of variation — it does not remove **sampling variation in the cases themselves**. A 1.5-point difference on 1,200 cases can arise from which cases happen to be in the set, and from run-to-run variation in the model's outputs. So the honest move is to report the difference together with an uncertainty estimate and state the decision rule before you look. This is the substance of Anthropic's eval guidance: define success criteria and a comparison method in advance, and be willing to say a difference is not distinguishable from noise. What you must not do is treat a bare point estimate as a release gate.

whyWrong.B: Using the same set makes the comparison paired, which reduces some noise — but it does not make the gap significant. The intuition that a controlled comparison guarantees a real difference is the most common way teams ship changes that do nothing, and it also means small regressions get waved through on the same logic.
whyWrong.C: There is no such convention, and a fixed 10-point threshold is arbitrary in the opposite direction: it would block a large, cheap, reliable improvement in a high-volume task while accepting a statistically meaningless 12-point swing on a small set. The threshold has to come from the decision's risk profile and the eval set's size, not from folklore.
whyWrong.D: A significance rule is the right shape, but a bare 95% threshold applied mechanically is not a complete policy — it ignores effect size, the cost of a false positive versus a false negative in this specific deployment, and whether the eval set is representative of production. For a high-consequence decision you would want a higher bar and a defined cost of being wrong in each direction.

questions.mindset: Never gate a release on a bare point estimate — report the difference with an uncertainty estimate and state the decision rule before looking.

questions.stem: A team improved a claims-triage prompt by adding the twelve cases it failed most often as few-shot examples. Overall accuracy rose from 84% to 95%, and the change is going into production. What is the MOST important caveat?

options.text: The eval set now contains the training cases, so the reported improvement is optimistic and the set has stopped being able to detect further overfitting; hold out a set of cases that was never used for prompt work, and add production failures to it over time.
Few-shot examples increase prompt length and therefore cost, so the improvement should be re-checked against a per-document cost ceiling before release.
An 11-point gain is large enough that a holdout is unnecessary; the magnitude of the improvement itself demonstrates the examples are representative.
The examples should be ordered so the most recent failures come last, since the model attends most strongly to the end of a long prompt.

questions.explanation: The failure mode here is textbook **evaluation contamination**, and it is the single most common way a large reported gain turns out to be partly illusory. Adding the cases you failed to the prompt and then measuring on a set that contains them means you are partly measuring recall of the examples rather than generalisation — so 95% overstates what the prompt will do on cases nobody has looked at. The second half is the part that is easy to miss and matters more: once the eval set doubles as the tuning set, it can no longer **detect** further overfitting, so the team's measurement instrument degrades exactly when they most rely on it. The fix is a held-out set plus a standing process for adding production failures — which keeps the instrument honest as the system evolves.

whyWrong.B: Prompt length and cost are real considerations and this is a legitimate operational concern — but it is a secondary point that does not threaten the validity of the measurement, whereas contamination does. Worth checking; not the most important caveat.
whyWrong.C: This inverts the logic entirely, and it is a tempting thing to believe when a number looks exciting. A large gain on a contaminated set is exactly what overfitting looks like: the magnitude reflects how much of the eval set was memorised, not how general the improvement is. The size of the gain tells you nothing about whether it will hold on new cases.
whyWrong.D: Position within a prompt can matter, so this is not a silly operational question — but it is a micro-optimisation being offered as the important caveat for a measurement-validity problem. Ordering examples is worth an experiment; it does not address whether the eval can still detect overfitting.

questions.mindset: The moment you add failing cases to the prompt you have contaminated the eval set — hold out cases that were never used for tuning.

questions.stem: A fintech is comparing two prompt versions for an assistant that explains a user's transaction history. There is no reference answer. Variant B scores higher with an LLM judge against a written rubric, and higher again on a second judge model. The team is about to ship. Which TWO additional pieces of evidence would the architect require before shipping? Choose TWO.

options.text: A blind human review of a sample, where reviewers do not see which variant produced each answer, since agreement between two models is not evidence about correctness.

An online test on real traffic with a business outcome as the metric — for example whether users stop asking the same question again — since an offline judge score is a proxy and the thing that matters is whether the explanation resolves the user's question.
A third judge model, so that the comparison is based on a majority of three graders rather than two, which reduces the risk of a shared blind spot.
Confirmation that variant B's answers are longer, since more detailed explanations are more likely to be rated as more helpful by any grader.
Re-running the comparison with the two judges' scores swapped between variants, which controls for any position bias in the grading order.

questions.explanation: Two independent model judges agreeing is **consistency**, not correctness — the judges share training lineage, prompt conventions and failure modes, and can be confidently wrong together. So the two things the architect should require are the two that supply evidence from outside that shared distribution. (A) is a blind human review: humans reading both variants without knowing which is which remove both grader bias and the position effect, and for a customer-facing explanation a hundred human reads is cheap and decisive. (B) closes the loop to reality — an offline rubric score is a proxy for ‘the user got what they needed’, and only a real-traffic outcome measures that. Anthropic's eval guidance is explicit that offline evals gate what you try and that online tests confirm what actually happened.

whyWrong.C: Adding a third model judge is the most available-looking way to increase confidence and it adds almost none. All three would be drawn from the same family with the same tendencies, so majority voting among them reduces variance around a shared bias rather than correcting it. It also costs a third of the grading budget to re-derive the same kind of answer.
whyWrong.D: This is a confounder dressed as a finding. If B is longer and graders prefer length — a well-documented tendency — then the score difference may be measuring verbosity rather than usefulness, which means shipping B makes explanations worse while the dashboard says better. Length should be checked and held roughly constant between variants, not used as supporting evidence.
whyWrong.E: Swapping the order in which variants are presented is a real technique and worth doing — but the stem already says the team compared them, and the bigger risk here is not position bias in a pairwise comparison but shared judge blind spots, which reordering cannot touch. It is hygiene, not evidence.

questions.mindset: Two model judges agreeing is consistency, not correctness — require blind human review and a real-traffic outcome before shipping.

questions.stem: A document-extraction service returns JSON that is occasionally missing the last few fields, always on documents longer than about four pages. Downstream validation catches it. What is the BEST first action?

options.text: Check the `stop_reason` on the affected responses — a response that ends with `max_tokens` was truncated mid-object, which points at output budget rather than at prompt quality, and the fix is to raise `max_tokens`, shorten the schema, or split long documents.
Add few-shot examples of complete long-document extractions, since the model is not producing enough output for inputs this long.
Move to the most capable Claude model with extended thinking, since long-document extraction is a reasoning task the current tier under-serves.
Add a Claude call after extraction that compares the parsed JSON against the source text and adds any missing fields, so the service self-heals before validation.

questions.explanation: The symptom — valid JSON that is **incomplete**, correlated with document length — is the signature of truncation, and the documented way to confirm it in one step is `stop_reason`: a response that ends with `max_tokens` ran out of output budget rather than deciding to stop. That single check moves this from speculation to diagnosis, and the fixes that follow are cheap and specific: raise `max_tokens`, or reduce what has to be emitted by flattening the schema, or split long documents so each extraction emits a bounded amount. This is the discipline the exam rewards — read the documented signal before reaching for a bigger model or a longer prompt.

whyWrong.B: Examples shape *behaviour*, and this is not a behavioural shortcoming: the model was doing the right thing and ran out of room. Adding examples of long complete extractions lengthens the prompt and can make truncation slightly more likely by consuming input budget, and it will not change the output ceiling.
whyWrong.C: A larger model with extended thinking is the reflex escalation and it addresses nothing in the evidence. If the response is being cut off at `max_tokens`, no amount of reasoning capacity produces the missing tokens — and thinking consumes budget, which can make truncation worse. It also raises cost and latency on every long document to fix a configuration limit.
whyWrong.D: A self-healing post-pass is the attractive ‘make it robust’ answer and it is strictly worse than fixing the cause: it doubles cost and latency on the hard documents, the repair pass reads the same source the first pass did and can introduce its own errors, and the underlying truncation remains — so the same failure will appear somewhere validation does not catch. Note that the team should still add a validation-and-retry loop as a second line of defence, but not as the first action.

questions.mindset: Read `stop_reason` before reaching for a bigger model — a response ending in `max_tokens` was truncated, and that is a budget problem.

questions.stem: A research assistant answers questions from a curated internal library. Reviewers find about 6% of answers assert something the source documents do not support — confident, specific, and wrong. The assistant is instructed to answer only from the supplied passages and to say it cannot answer when they are insufficient. Which TWO changes would the architect expect to reduce the rate MOST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Make attribution part of the output contract — require the answer to cite the specific passage for each claim, with citations verified against the retrieved context before the answer is returned, so an unsupported assertion has nothing to attach to.

Restrict retrieval to a smaller number of higher-confidence passages and pass them with an explicit instruction that each answer must be fully supported by the passages provided, so fewer irrelevant passages compete for the answer.
Move to the most capable Claude model, since hallucination rate tracks model capability and the current tier is the main limitation.
Add a second pass where Claude reviews each answer against the passages and rewrites it if any claim is unsupported, since self-review is a direct mitigation for hallucination.
Lower the temperature to the minimum and set `top_p` low, since sampling nondeterminism is the cause of confident fabrications.

questions.explanation: The two changes that address hallucination in a grounded task both act on **what the answer has to do** rather than on how capable the model is. (A) makes grounding structural: if every claim must carry a citation and the citation is checked against the retrieved context, an unsupported assertion cannot be produced without something to point at — and Anthropic's documented hallucination guidance recommends exactly this, citing sources so claims can be verified. Citations also convert the failure from invisible to attributable, which is what makes it measurable. (B) attacks the mechanism: hallucination in RAG is usually driven by irrelevant or partially-relevant passages in context, so tightening retrieval and stating the support requirement addresses the cause. The theme is worth naming — the most reliable reductions come from constraints and verification, not from hoping the model is smarter.

whyWrong.C: Capability is the most intuitive lever and the weakest. Model choice does affect hallucination rates, but a stronger model in the same architecture still produces unsupported claims from insufficient context — it just does so less often, at higher cost, and the failure mode remains silent. The stem's 6% is specific claims the sources do not support, which is a grounding problem.
whyWrong.D: Self-review is the most attractive answer because it names the right technique (verify the answer against the source) but applies it wrongly. A model reviewing its own answer has no information the first pass lacked — if it believed the claim while writing it, it usually still believes it while reviewing — so you pay double cost for a second opinion from the same reader. Verification should be a check against something external: the passages, a deterministic field check, or a human.
whyWrong.E: Sampling parameters are about diversity, not truthfulness. A temperature of zero makes the model more *consistent*, and a consistently wrong answer is exactly the failure mode here — 6% of confident, specific, wrong claims. It also does nothing about whether the retrieved passages support the answer at all.

questions.mindset: Reduce hallucination with grounding constraints and verifiable attribution — a stronger model, lower temperature or self-review do not fix unsupported claims.

questions.stem: An IT service desk uses Claude to classify tickets as ‘incident’ or ‘service request’. Overall accuracy is 94%, but on tickets written in informal language with screenshots and no error text it drops to 71%, and the service desk manager says those are 40% of real volume. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Add labelled informal, screenshot-bearing tickets to the eval set as a distinct stratum, then fix the gap — most likely by giving the classifier access to the ticket's system metadata (affected service, alert history) rather than the free-text alone, since the information needed to classify is present in the systems and absent from the message.
Report the disaggregated accuracy to the steering group and accept 71% on that stratum, since 94% overall already meets the agreed threshold and the threshold was set on the aggregate.
Retrain the classifier on a larger set of informal tickets, since the informal cases need more examples of that style before the model will classify them correctly.
Switch to a stronger Claude model, since the informal stratum is harder and the current tier cannot handle vague, screenshot-only descriptions.

questions.explanation: The 94% aggregate is measured against a threshold, but the stratum in question is **40% of real volume** — so this is not a long tail, it is the majority-adjacent case the threshold was never designed to cover. (A) does the two things needed: it puts the failure in the eval set as its own stratum so the gap is visible and trackable, and it identifies the likely cause — the classifier is being asked to decide from a message that does not contain the deciding information. A ticket saying ‘[image] still broken??’ carries no error text; the affected service and alert history do. Adding those as inputs fixes the information problem rather than the model. This is the same principle as the earlier questions: measure at the granularity where the error lives, and prefer to give the pipeline the information it lacks over asking the model to infer it.

whyWrong.B: This is the answer the exam is built to catch — accepting an aggregate number that conceals the majority case. The threshold was agreed as an aggregate, and the honest architectural move when a measurement turns out to be mis-specified is to renegotiate it with evidence, not to invoke it. A service desk that misclassifies 29% of its informal tickets will accumulate incidents that are actually requests, which is precisely the workload the project was meant to reduce.
whyWrong.C: More informal examples help if the problem is that the model does not know the style, and adding them to the eval set is part of (A). But style is not the issue — the content is. ‘[image] still broken??’ is short and there is very little to learn from thousands of such examples; what is missing is the affected-service information, which no volume of free-text examples will supply. Fine-tuning a classifier is also a large commitment when the fix is an input.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model is a plausible step-up and it may improve the informal stratum somewhat. It is not the best answer because it addresses capability when the evidence points at missing input — and because escalating to a larger model across 100% of volume, to fix 40% of it, is an expensive answer to a problem that adding one metadata field addresses. Establish the cause before paying for capacity.

questions.mindset: When an aggregate metric conceals a large stratum, disaggregate, then fix the missing information in the pipeline before escalating the model.

questions.stem: A customer-support assistant answers well but produces three- or four-paragraph replies where two sentences would do, inflating output token cost and making the chat feel heavy. Which change addresses this MOST directly?

options.text: Specify the length and shape in the output contract — a maximum word count with a required structure (one direct answer, then at most two supporting sentences) — and enforce it in code against `max_tokens`, since brevity is a requirement to be stated and checked rather than a style the model will infer.
Lower `max_tokens`, which caps output length directly and therefore reduces both cost and verbosity without touching the prompt.
Add few-shot examples of concise replies, since examples are the most reliable way to control output style.
Move to a cheaper model tier, since a less capable model writes shorter answers and the current tier's verbosity is a side effect of its quality.

questions.explanation: Length is a **requirement**, and the reliable way to handle a requirement is to state it and check it. (A) does both: the prompt specifies the structure and budget, and the code-side check against `max_tokens` catches a response that ignored it — at which point you have a retry or a truncation decision, which is a known quantity, rather than a bill. It is also the only option that shapes the *content* rather than just the ceiling: ‘one direct answer, then at most two supporting sentences— tells the model what to cut, which is the actual problem. Verbosity in an assistant usually comes from a prompt that has not said what to omit.

whyWrong.B: Lowering `max_tokens` is the tempting one-token fix and it does cut cost, but it caps length without shaping it — so replies get truncated mid-sentence and the assistant looks broken. The earlier question in this domain covers exactly this failure. `max_tokens` is a safety ceiling, not a length specification.
whyWrong.C: Examples are indeed effective at controlling style and they are the right second step. They are not the MOST direct fix here because the stem says nothing about whether the prompt specifies length at all — and if it does not, adding examples is an indirect way to specify what should be stated outright. Fix the contract first; use examples to reinforce it.
whyWrong.D: A cheaper model writing shorter answers is a correlation, not a mechanism, and the trade is bad — you give up quality you have already verified across every other dimension to obtain brevity by accident. If brevity is a requirement it belongs in the contract, where it is deliberate and testable.

questions.mindset: Length is a requirement: state it in the output contract, enforce it in code against `max_tokens`, and use examples to reinforce it.

questions.stem: A legal-tech firm's contract-review service sends a 30,000-token stable policy-and-playbook prefix on every request with `cache_control` on it, followed by the contract. Finance reports the bill nearly doubled last month. Which TWO explanations should the architect investigate FIRST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Whether the cache is actually hitting — the prefix is stable but requests arrive on a fleet of API keys and a rotating pool of workers, so an unstable cache identifier or fragmented key usage means writes are charged without reads, which would show up as exactly this cost pattern.

Whether traffic volume or document size grew, since cached input is billed at a lower rate but not free, and a doubling can simply be more contracts or longer ones — cost models must start from volume multiplied by tokens per request.
Whether the prompt has been edited recently, since changing any part of the cached prefix invalidates the whole prefix and the next request pays full price for all 30,000 tokens.
Whether the team should move the service to the Message Batches API, since batch is the documented mechanism for reducing the cost of high-volume Claude workloads.
Whether the model tier was changed, since a newer model generation may price output tokens differently from the tier the budget was built on.

questions.explanation: The bill doubled while the architecture is unchanged, so the architect is looking for causes that produce **exactly this signature** without a code change — and the two strongest are both about the cache prefix. (A) is the classic operational cause: caching only pays off when subsequent requests present the same prefix, so a fleet rotating API keys or workers, or an unstable identifier, means you write the prefix repeatedly and rarely read it — and cache writes are charged at a premium over base input, which is why the bill goes **up** rather than merely failing to go down. (C) is the content cause: any edit anywhere in the prefix invalidates the whole thing from that point, so a routine prompt tweak can silently convert 30,000 tokens per request into full-price input. Both are checkable from usage data before anything is changed.

whyWrong.D: Moving to the Batches API is a substantial architectural change — it requires that nobody is waiting, and this is an interactive contract-review service — and it should be considered on its own merits, not as a diagnosis. Batch pricing is not the explanation for a change in a synchronous workload's cost, and it would be a large, risky move to make before establishing why the current design's cost moved.
whyWrong.E: A model or pricing change is worth checking and is a routine part of cost review. It is not among the two to investigate *first* here, because the prefix is 30,000 tokens of input per request — the input side dominates a contract-review workload's cost, so the cache behaviour on that prefix is where a doubling is most likely to originate. Also note that a tier change would be visible in the deployment record, whereas cache misses are invisible.
whyWrong.B: Volume growth is always worth checking and the cost model should start there — but as an *explanation of a doubling* it is the least interesting option, because it presumes no regression and the stem says nothing about volume changing. If volume doubled, nobody would be asking. The question is what changed in a system whose architecture did not.

questions.mindset: When a cached workload's cost rises without a code change, suspect cache misses — unstable keys, edited prefixes — before changing the architecture.

questions.stem: A finance director reads that the Message Batches API offers substantially lower per-token pricing and asks the architect to move the company's live customer-facing chat assistant onto it. What is the architect's answer?

options.text: No — the chat assistant is interactive, so a customer is waiting for every reply and batch mode's turnaround is incompatible with that. Batch suits work with a latency tolerance, such as nightly summarisation; for this workload the cost levers are caching, model tier and output length.
Yes, provided the assistant streams results, since streaming is what makes a batch response feel interactive to the customer.
Yes, but only for the follow-up summarisation step, so that the live reply stays synchronous while the background write-up runs in batch mode.
Yes, if the assistant pre-computes likely replies for common questions at build time, so that most customer requests are served from cache while rarer ones go through batch mode.

questions.explanation: Batch mode trades turnaround for price, so the deciding question is the one from the cost-and-latency material: **is anyone waiting?** A customer is waiting for every chat reply, so batch is structurally wrong here — no amount of engineering makes an asynchronous submission feel like a conversation. And the cost problem is still real, so the architect points at the levers that do apply to an interactive workload: caching the stable system prefix, routing routine intents to a cheaper tier with escalation, and controlling output length. That combination is where interactive savings come from.

whyWrong.B: Streaming and the Message Batches API are unrelated mechanisms — streaming is how tokens are delivered within a single response, while batch is how requests are submitted and collected. You cannot stream a batch submission, and mixing up the two is one of the more common misconceptions in cost conversations.
whyWrong.C: This is a sensible-sounding compromise and it is a real optimisation — but it is not what was asked and it does not help the live chat path at all, which is the workload with the latency constraint and therefore the one carrying the per-interaction cost. Worth doing as a separate improvement; not an answer to moving the chat assistant.
whyWrong.D: Precomputing common replies is a legitimate caching strategy, and batch for rare queries is worse than a synchronous call for rare queries — you have accepted a worse experience for exactly the cases you know least about. The design also inverts the risk: the precomputed answers are the ones most likely to be stale, since they are frozen at build time.

questions.mindset: Ask who is waiting — batch pricing never applies to a live conversation; use caching, tiering and output length for interactive workloads.

questions.stem: A long-running operations agent calls an inventory API that returns about 60 fields per item, of which the agent uses 5. Over a 40-step session, early results push earlier ones out of the window, and the agent begins re-querying for information it once had. Which TWO changes address the root cause? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have the tool return only the fields the task needs — or accept a field list as an argument — so each result is a fraction of the size, because the waste here is structural: 55 unused fields on every call is the mechanism that crowds the window.
Enable context editing or compaction so that stale tool results are summarised or dropped as the session proceeds, keeping the recent turns and the durable facts while reclaiming the window.
Raise `max_tokens` so the window can hold all 40 steps of results, since the agent is running out of room rather than out of signal.
Persist the inventory state to the scratchpad as the agent works, so that earlier lookups are recorded in a form that survives compaction rather than living only in the transcript.
Split the session into a summariser agent and an executor agent, so that one compacts and the other acts.

questions.explanation: The mechanism is stated plainly in the stem: **55 of every 60 fields are unused**, so the tool's return shape is the root cause and (A) removes it at the source. This is the right order of attack — fixing the producer beats filtering at the consumer, and it also cuts latency, since fewer tokens are generated and transmitted. (D) is the second structural change and it addresses the *other* half: even with leaner results, a 40-step session accumulates state that eventually gets compacted, and once that happens anything living only in the transcript is gone — which is exactly the re-querying behaviour described. Persisting durable state outside the transcript means compaction is survivable. Together they mean the session stays both small and recoverable.

whyWrong.B: Context editing and compaction are real, documented capabilities and they genuinely reclaim window in a long session — so an architect would raise this. It is not one of the two that address the **root cause** here: it treats the symptom by discarding 55-fields-per-result data the agent never needed, and compaction of useless data still costs a summarisation call. It is the right complement to (A) and (D), not a substitute.
whyWrong.C: The agent is not running out of model capacity — it is running out of context window, which is a fixed budget you cannot raise for a given model. Raising `max_tokens` controls how much the model *generates*, not how much it can *read*, so this does not address the problem at all. It is a common and total misreading of the two parameters.
whyWrong.E: Adding an agent to summarise another agent's context is the maximally automated answer and it is the wrong shape: it introduces a second context that can itself fill, adds a model call per compaction, and puts a summariser between the agent and the state it needs. Compaction is a built-in capability; the durable-state fix in (D) is the architectural one.

questions.mindset: When a long session overflows, fix the producer's return shape first, then persist durable state outside the transcript so compaction is survivable.

questions.stem: A retailer's support dashboard shows request volume, HTTP error rate and average latency — all healthy for two months. Customer satisfaction has fallen steadily. The support lead asks what to add. What is the MOST useful monitoring change?

options.text: Break quality metrics out by dimension — intent, language, product line and account tier — rather than reporting one fleet-wide average, because the same aggregate that stays flat while satisfaction falls is precisely the aggregate that cannot see a deteriorating segment.
Add a thumbs-up and thumbs-down control to every conversation, so satisfaction can be measured directly rather than inferred.
Add an LLM-judge score over a daily sample of production answers against a written rubric, so answer quality becomes a tracked metric.
Lower the alert threshold on API error rate, so the team is warned earlier about degradation.

questions.explanation: The diagnostic clue is that the **aggregate is flat while the outcome is falling** — which means the information the team has is structurally incapable of seeing the problem. Segmenting is the fix: by intent, language, product line and tier, one of those cuts will show the decline while the others stay flat, and that cut names the cause. This is the same principle as the disaggregated-accuracy questions elsewhere in this domain, and it is the monitoring counterpart of per-group evaluation floors. (B) and (C) both add overall satisfaction and quality signals, which is progress — but a single fleet-wide satisfaction number declines for the same reason the latency average did not: it averages away the segment. (D) tightens a threshold on a metric that has been healthy throughout.

whyWrong.B: A thumbs control is a genuine and cheap signal and it belongs on the dashboard. It is not the most useful addition here, because opt-in ratings are sparse and heavily self-selected — raters skew to the extremes — so the resulting number would also be an aggregate over a biased population and would fall slowly and ambiguously, telling the team that something is wrong without telling them where.
whyWrong.C: An LLM-judge quality score is a strong addition and arguably the most valuable of the three signal options — it measures the thing customers actually react to. It is still fleet-wide by default, so it inherits the same blindness; and the stem's existing metrics are all fleet-wide and all flat. Add it, then **segment it** — which is what (A) says to do with any quality metric you add.
whyWrong.D: Lowering a threshold on a metric that has been healthy for two months adds alert noise without adding information. The problem is not that the team is being warned too late about API errors; it is that API errors are not where the failure is.

questions.mindset: When an aggregate is flat while the outcome falls, the aggregate is structurally blind — segment quality metrics by intent, language, line and tier.

questions.stem: A team wants to instrument its Claude API integration for debugging, and asks Anthropic support for help with a specific failed request. What must the team have captured in order for support to be able to help?

options.text: The `request-id` returned with the failed response, plus the approximate time of the failure — which means logging it on every request, because it cannot be recovered once the response is gone.
The complete prompt and response text, since support will need to see the exact content to understand the failure.
The API key and the workspace identifier, so support can confirm the account has access to the model being used.
The application's stack trace from the HTTP client, since most failures originate in the client library rather than the API.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's error documentation directs you to support with the **`request-id`** and the time window, because that id is the handle used to locate the request in the provider's own logs. The architectural consequence is the part to take away: the id is only useful if it was logged when the request happened, so correlation identifiers belong permanently in the request path — a small, permanent addition that pays for itself the first time something fails. It is worth noting that support does not need, and should not receive, your prompt content or your credentials, which keeps a debugging relationship from becoming a data-exfiltration path.

whyWrong.B: Support cannot run your prompt, and sending full request content into a support channel creates a second copy of data that may include personal or regulated information. It also does not help correlate to a specific request server-side, which is what the request id is for.
whyWrong.C: An API key must never be sent to anyone. A workspace identifier is useful context; the key is not, and an account that lacks model access receives an authorisation error rather than an intermittent 500.
whyWrong.D: A client stack trace is useful for diagnosing your own code, and most 5xx errors will not have one. But it does not let support locate the request in provider-side logs, which is the specific thing the request id enables.

questions.mindset: Log the provider's request-id on every call from day one; it is the only handle support has and it cannot be recovered later.

questions.stem: An e-commerce assistant's weekly LLM-judge score is flat, its error rate is flat, and its cost per request is flat. A new product line launched last month and its customers file complaints that other customers do not. Which monitoring addition would MOST reliably catch this class of problem?

options.text: Sample production traffic continuously with the judge scored per product line and per intent, and alert on a segment-level drop rather than the fleet mean — because the fleet mean is structurally incapable of detecting a new segment's problems, and a launch is a change in traffic composition, not a change in system behaviour.
Re-run the offline eval suite weekly against a fixed test set, so that a regression introduced by the new product line is caught by the regression gate.
Add the new product line's questions to the existing eval set immediately, since the eval set should reflect everything the system now handles.
Increase the sampling rate of the production judge from 1% to 10%, since the current rate is too low to detect a meaningful number of affected conversations.

questions.explanation: The failure class here is a **change in traffic composition** — the system did not get worse, a new kind of question arrived — and no fleet-wide metric can see that, because averaging over a larger, differently-shaped population keeps the mean in place. (A) is the design that catches it: sample continuously, score **per segment**, and alert at the segment level, so the new product line's score falls while the overall average does not move. Note that the same principle governs the judge's rubric — if the rubric was written only for the original product lines, the new line is being judged by criteria that do not describe it, which is another reason per-segment scoring matters.

whyWrong.B: A weekly regression eval is genuinely good practice and it catches changes the team made. It cannot catch this, because the new product line's questions were never in the fixed test set — so the suite runs, passes, and the complaints continue. It is also orthogonal to the production symptom: the team has complaints about live traffic, and an offline suite only tells you about the cases it contains.
whyWrong.C: Adding the cases is right in principle — but the stem's problem is that the failure is happening in production and is invisible, not that the eval set is unaware of the product line. Fixing the eval set improves future release decisions while leaving this complaint stream unexplained, and it does not tell you which conversations are going wrong now. That needs production sampling, segmented.
whyWrong.D: Raising the sample rate makes an existing measurement more precise; it does not change what that measurement is aggregated over. At 10% fleet-wide the new product line is still averaged into the whole, so the signal is still diluted — and it is worth recalling that in most products fewer than 1% of sessions get rated at all, so the binding constraint here is segment coverage, not volume. Sampling wider is not sampling smarter.

questions.mindset: A launch changes traffic composition, not system behaviour — sample production traffic and alert per segment, not on the fleet mean.

questions.stem: A hospital's discharge-summarisation assistant is evaluated before go-live. The medical director wants one confidence figure. The architect proposes three metrics: a clinician-rated completeness score, a harm-weighted error rate on the medication list, and a ‘would a clinician send this without editing?’ rate. Which statement about these is MOST accurate?

options.text: They measure different things and none of them is a confidence figure: completeness is coverage, the harm-weighted rate is severity, and the send-without-editing rate is workflow fit. A single number would average a fatal error with a missing courtesy line, and the harm-weighted rate should be a hard gate while the others track improvement.
They are redundant measures of the same underlying quality, so reporting the mean of the three gives a more stable single figure than any one of them alone.
The harm-weighted error rate is the only one worth measuring in a clinical setting, since clinical risk is the sole concern and the other two measure preferences.
They should be combined into a weighted single score agreed with the medical director, since regulators and boards expect one headline number for each governed system.

questions.explanation: The stem's ‘one confidence figure’ request is the thing to push back on, and (A) is why: these are three **different properties**, and collapsing them into one number destroys the information that makes them actionable. A medication error and a missing courtesy sentence are not commensurable, so any average of them is a number whose meaning depends on the weighting chosen — which means the average is set by whoever picks the weights, not by the evidence. The architect's better move is to say what each number *is for*: severity as a hard release gate, coverage and workflow fit as tracked trends that show where editing effort is going. That is a defensible position to take into a governance meeting, and it is the difference between a metric set and a vanity number.

whyWrong.B: Averaging non-commensurable measures is the standard way to produce a number that moves for reasons nobody can explain. The three metrics are not noisy repetitions of one latent quantity — a summary can be complete and require heavy editing, or edit-free and omit something important — so they carry genuinely independent information that averaging destroys.
whyWrong.C: Severity should dominate and should gate the release, but the other two are not preferences. Workflow fit is an operational and safety signal in its own right: a summary clinicians rewrite every time trains them to ignore the tool, and coverage tells you which document types are under-served — which is how you find the next medication-list failure before a clinician does.
whyWrong.D: A single weighted score is what boards ask for and it is the right thing to give them **alongside** the underlying metrics, not instead of them. The failure is in the ‘agreed with the medical director’ framing as a substitute: the weights become a negotiation about presentation, and a system can then pass its headline number while its worst-severity metric is unacceptable — unless the severity metric is a separate hard gate, which is what (A) says.

questions.mindset: Keep severity as a hard gate and coverage and workflow fit as tracked trends — averaging non-commensurable risks produces a meaningless headline.

questions.stem: A financial-services firm runs several Claude features across four teams. Finance wants per-team monthly spend reported automatically, with an alert at 80% of budget. Security says no prompt text, no customer data and no document content may leave the team's own boundary, but token counts and model identifiers are acceptable. Which approach meets both?

options.text: Expose usage through the platform's own metering — token counts, model id, and a low-cardinality team or cost-centre attribute on each request — with budgets and alerts configured against that, so the finance data is derived from request metadata and no content is collected anywhere.
Log each request and response to a shared analytics store with a team tag, then aggregate spend there, since the data already exists and only needs to be joined.
Have each team run its own local proxy that counts tokens and posts a monthly total to the finance system, since a local proxy guarantees content never leaves the boundary.
Reconcile spend from the provider's invoice, which lists usage at the account level, and have each team confirm their own share at month end.

questions.explanation: The constraint pair — automatic per-team attribution with **no content leaving the boundary** — points at metadata rather than content. (A) works because spend is a function of token counts and model identity, neither of which is customer data: you can compute a per-team figure from request metadata alone, which is exactly why security can accept it. The low-cardinality team attribute is what makes the attribution possible at all, and it has to be attached by the team that owns the request rather than reconstructed later. Budgets and alerts then become configuration against a metric that already exists, so there is no new pipeline to maintain and no new exposure.

whyWrong.B: This is the obvious implementation and it violates the security constraint outright — request and response bodies contain the prompt and the answer, which is customer data. The note that ‘the data already exists’ is the trap: it exists inside the boundary where it belongs, and copying it to a shared store to compute a number that token counts already give you is an unnecessary exposure of exactly the data that must not move.
whyWrong.C: A local proxy is a defensible architecture for organisations that need to inspect or route content, and it does keep content local. It is not the best answer because it is a bespoke component to build, run and secure per team, when the requirement — spend by team — needs no content at all. It also does not solve the harder half of the problem well: a hand-rolled proxy has no visibility into the Agent SDK and MCP calls that drive much of a team's actual spend.
whyWrong.D: Reconciling from an account-level invoice cannot produce a per-team figure — the invoice is the total, which is precisely the number nobody can act on. Asking teams to self-report at month end makes the data retrospective, unauditable and dependent on everyone's recollection, and it arrives after the budget has already been exceeded.

questions.mindset: Derive per-team cost from request metadata — token counts and a cost-centre label — so finance gets attribution without collecting any content.
